newsitem.title: UK: Strike grounds hundreds of BA flights.
newsitem.headline: Strike grounds hundreds of BA flights.

text.p: Striking cabin crew forced British Airways to cancel half its flights out of London Wednesday, leaving more than 25,000 passengers stranded.

As the strike forced the cancellation of between 20 percent and 30 percent of the 1,000 flights it operates worldwide each day, the airline said it had consulted its lawyers because it believed the action was illegal.
"We are now in active discussions with our legal advisers," said Mervyn Walker, BA director of human resources, adding that there were discrepancies in the strike ballot that made it illegal.
"We have the right to damages in respect of losses we incur, and to other legal remedies."

The airline's Heathrow Airport hub bore the brunt of the disruption from the three-day strike, with less than one in three flights able to go ahead. BA said that 70 percent to 80 percent of its flights would operate, after a company spokeswoman earlier said just 20 percent of its flights would take off.
The airline said newspaper reports that a breakthrough could be made through the appointment of an independent arbiter were "inaccurate."
Members of the T&G began the strike early Wednesday in the face of warnings by management that strikers would lose perks and face a lockout unless they promised to work normally in the future.
BA insisted it would not negotiate the terms of a deal to cut costs by 42 million pounds ($71 million).
The union has said it was prepared to help the airline find the money, but it was not prepared to have new terms and conditions imposed on its members.
It also disputed BA's claim that the 72-hour strike that was to continue until Saturday morning is illegal.

"We have absolute confidence in the legality of our conduct," union spokesman Andrew Murray told Reuters, adding that the union was still willing to negotiate. "There is no change in the union position."
British travel agents were flooded with calls from customers trying to find alternative flights on rival airlines.
U.S. airlines said they would try to help passengers and cargo stranded by the strike but warned that there was limited extra space during the hectic summer travel season.
British Airways said late Wednesday that 874 cabin staff had reported to work as normal and it expected the number to increase to about 1,000 by the end of the day.
More than 1,500 called in sick, rather than strike, because of fears of crossing a picket line. Another 160 have been officially on strike.
The airline needs 1,800 to 2,000 staff to run a full programme on a normal day.
"It is clear to us now that the strike is not well supported," said Kevin Murray, BA director of communications. "A large number of crew are coming into work."

Asked whether the crew had reported sick rather than go on strike because of BA's threats that strikers would lose perks and face a lockout, Walker said: "Crew have not been threatened. We have not intimidated and never would intimidate any of our employees."
